text: Dogfight Chapter 1: Tagging the Predator The trial ended in blood and silence. Hooks stood empty. Survivors bled into the Fog, their screams already dissolving in the distance, as they always did. Wesker stood tall amid the wreckage of smashed pallets and discarded medkits that littered the admin desk of Lery’s, chest heaving — not from exertion, more from restraint. Uroboros still pulsed under his skin like a tethered storm, hungry and writhing. There was often a kind of tension hangover after a match; the bloodlust from the fight never quite bleeding off right away even when there was nothing left to throw, but no good would come of taking it out on the surroundings. Best to just head home and wait it out. He tilted his head, waiting. The Entity should have pulled him by now, tugging him back to the RPD station in that familiar haze of static unraveling. She was taking her time today, it seemed. Not totally unusual; some days the Entity took longer than others to extract her killers, and it really wasn’t often that he got the chance to stretch out in another domain like this. He stilled, every sense straining. Nothing moved. Even the crows were gone. The calm should have been satisfying — a clean hunt, quota met — but the stillness was itching at him regardless, driving him to idly pace the halls while he waited. The halls were gray with dust, the sky out the stained windows a smear of barely visible light. Each footstep came back to him a fraction late, like the echo of a heartbeat out of rhythm. He followed the sound anyway, pacing through the ruin simply because doing nothing felt worse. The air pressed thicker the further he went, heavy with heat. Something sharp lived inside it, a scent vaguely under the rust and rot: copper, antiseptic... sweetness. He took it in, curious, before he realized he shouldn’t have. It burned faintly, a chemical perfume that clung to the back of his throat. He winced, annoyed, and kept moving. The smell followed. He hadn’t noticed it during the hunt, entirely too wrapped up in the angles and vaults to really take in the ambient smell of the center. Now that he had nothing else to focus on, it was everywhere. A prickle crept up his neck. The Fog’s edges shimmered — too bright, too alive. His skin tightened, pupils contracting to pinpoints as Uroboros stirred under his ribs. He felt watched despite the emptiness of the hallways. No matter how hard he listened, there was nothing to sense. He was positive that he was alone. Still, this felt... wrong. He turned once more, scanning the perimeter, but the world looked subtly warped — colors shifting toward a feverish spectrum, shapes sliding where they should have held. His breath hitched, shallow. Heat rippled down his spine. The viral hum inside him spiked in answer, apparently just as restless. He hadn’t gone that much harder than normal this trial, had he? He would need to take a solid rest back at the station, provided the Entity left him be. Excessive fatigue wasn’t unheard of, but it had been a while since he had felt its effects; and he had been running trials back-to-back as of late with very little downtime between. Even a god needed a nap once in a while. Another breath. A sweetness on the air. Sickly-sweet. Something acrid curled in behind it, coating his tongue, dragging a cough up from deep in his chest. If the Fog didn’t take him home soon, he would need to wait out by the gate. Without the blood and bitter terror of the survivors, the institute really was impossible to linger in for long. What was taking Her so long, anyways? The halls were clearly dusted with her Fog, lightly coiling around broken pallets and doorframes, as if it somehow failed to notice he was even there still. His stance shifted. He stretched slightly, one hand lifting to adjust his coat as if warding off the unease, his fingers twitched before they could land. A tremor flickered through his arm, sharp and precise. The air around him moved slightly, a faint hiss like an exhale from the walls, almost polite. He recognized the sound instantly, the realization hitting like a slap. Not fatigue. He had wandered willingly straight into a trap. A second tremor. His foot skidded half a step, as if his leg had forgotten how to obey. The Fog around him thickened, something in his head tilting sharply sideways. His vision warped like light through oil, and a sudden weight pressed behind his eyes. "What—" His body pitched forward, catching himself against a nearby window vault. He drew another breath out of reflex and choked on it. The gas laced deep, threading nerves, short-circuiting synapses. The infection under his skin reacted violently, veins blooming black as it tried to purge the intrusion. His muscles trembled from the internal war. Wesker staggered, one hand braced against the wall, the other trying to ward off further contamination, burying his face in a sleeve. The hiss grew louder, seemingly from every wall now. A chemical cocktail working down into his blood, sneaking past Uroboros’ defenses before the virus could even identify the intrusion. He had wandered too far into the building to get back to the outside air of the gate. The timing had been exact. This wasn’t brute force. It was finesse. A slow bleed. A calculated takedown. “Show yourself!” The snarl broke halfway through, distorted by a spasm that clenched his jaw shut. Gold flared behind his eyes as the virus rose to meet the threat. For a moment he almost held it — the predator forcing the body upright through sheer defiance, every tendon drawn like wire.
